\subsection{Qwen2.5-7B Self-Reference Scale Probe}
\label{app:qwen7b_selfref}

The preceding 7--8B experiments (\S\ref{app:cross_scale_full}) use 4-bit NF4 QLoRA with Pythia-1.4B cross-reference, leaving two confounds unresolved: (1)~quantization-induced perplexity distortion and (2)~vocabulary mismatch between the 7B generator and the 1.4B reference model.
To isolate the scale effect from these artifacts, we run the full recursive generation pipeline on Qwen2.5-7B \cite{qwen2.5} (base model, not instruction-tuned) using FP16 LoRA fine-tuning and self-reference feature extraction (the same model serves as both generator and reference).

\paragraph{Setup.}
At each depth $k \in \{0, 1, 2, 3\}$, a fresh LoRA adapter ($r{=}16$, $\alpha{=}32$, dropout $0.05$, target modules \texttt{q\_proj}, \texttt{k\_proj}, \texttt{v\_proj}) is initialized on the base model and trained on $\mathcal{D}_{k-1}$ for 3 epochs (lr $2{\times}10^{-4}$, effective batch size 16 via $4 \times 4$ gradient accumulation, bfloat16 mixed precision), following the same protocol as the 1--1.5B benchmark (\S\ref{sec:method:benchmark}).
Generation uses nucleus sampling ($p{=}0.95$), producing 5{,}000 passages per depth (20{,}000 total, matching the per-cell sample size of the primary benchmark).
Feature extraction computes the standard 19-dimensional feature vector $\mathbf{f}(x)$ using the model's own token-level log-probabilities as the reference distribution, eliminating the cross-model reference artifact quantified in Table~\ref{tab:cross_ref_14b}.
Classification uses the same 5-fold stratified Random Forest (200 trees, seed 42) as all other cells.

\paragraph{Comparison to prior 7B experiments.}
This experiment differs from the QLoRA Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct entry in Table~\ref{tab:cross_scale} in three respects: (i)~FP16 LoRA removes quantization distortion, (ii)~self-reference removes vocabulary mismatch, and (iii)~5{,}000 samples per depth (vs.\ 500) narrows confidence intervals.
If depth signal persists under these cleaner conditions, the attenuation observed in the QLoRA experiments reflects genuine scale effects rather than methodological artifacts.

The preceding experiments assume a single model family generates all recursive depths.

\paragraph{Cross-model recursive chains.}
We construct a heterogeneous chain: human text (d0) $\to$ Pythia-1.4B generates d1 $\to$ OLMo-1B finetuned on Pythia-d1 generates d2 $\to$ GPT-2~XL finetuned on OLMo-d2 generates d3.
Each recursive step uses a \emph{different} model family, eliminating the possibility that depth signal arises from a single model's idiosyncratic behavior.

Pairwise AUC remains high: d0-vs-d1 = 0.999 and d2-vs-d3 = 0.841.
These results suggest that distributional artifacts of recursive generation persist across model boundaries. This constitutes preliminary evidence for a process-level depth signal rather than individual generator artifacts.

\section{Discussion and Conclusion}
\label{sec:discussion}

\paragraph{Multi-channel depth encoding.}
Four importance measures (Gini, SHAP, permutation, CPI; Kendall's $W{=}0.90$) converge on the same feature ranking, and Binoculars-derived features independently reach 78.1\%, not statistically distinguishable from 78.4\% (permutation $p{>}0.05$; merged: 82.6\%).
Depth signal is a distributional property encoded across multiple statistical channels; CORAL ordinal regression yields only marginal improvement (+0.3\,pp, Appendix~\ref{app:learned_estimator}), confirming ordinal structure is captured by the feature space rather than requiring specialized loss functions.

\paragraph{Why neural methods underperform.}
End-to-end classifiers (DeBERTa, RoBERTa-DCOL) lag RF by 14--33\,pp (\S\ref{sec:gen:baselines}) despite full token-level context, confirming that depth is encoded in distributional tail statistics that pretrained representations do not capture (d2 recall as low as 8\%); targeted feature engineering is necessary, not merely convenient.

\paragraph{Feature hierarchy across depths.}
The importance transition from \texttt{var\_surprisal} at shallow boundaries to perplexity tail statistics at deeper ones (\S\ref{sec:atlas:features}) mirrors tail-contraction dynamics: early recursion narrows the surprisal distribution while later steps erode the perplexity tail, consistent with geometric contraction (\S\ref{sec:method:theory}).

\paragraph{Deployment considerations.}
The strategy effect (9.3\,pp) exceeding the model effect (7.2\,pp) requires auditing pipelines to condition on decoding configuration (\S\ref{sec:gen:crossstrategy}), echoing \citet{schaeffer2025}.
Similarly, the pipeline relies on a fixed reference model (12/19 features from reference perplexity), with cross-architecture alternatives degrading by 4--11\,pp (Appendix~\ref{app:ref_ablation}); accuracy attenuation at 14B (\S\ref{sec:gen:crossscale}) may be partially recoverable via scale-matched references.

\paragraph{Accumulation and outlook.}
Depth estimation bridges binary detection and model collapse research by providing ordinal resolution \cite{drayson2025_detection_prevents_collapse}.
Accumulation experiments at 25--50\% synthetic mixing (Appendix~\ref{app:accumulation_auc}) partially validate depth estimation under realistic conditions: $\mathrm{EDD}_{0.70}{=}3$ is preserved in 5/6 cells, with only GPT-2~XL d2-vs-d3 marginally below threshold (AUC\,=\,0.695 vs.\ $T{=}0.70$).

\section{Related Work}
\label{sec:related}

\paragraph{Model Collapse Theory.}
Recursive training on model outputs erodes distributional tails \cite{shumailov2024_nature}, an effect formalized as exponential tail decay via scaling laws \cite{dohmatob2024_tale_of_tails,seddik2024synthetic} and extended to autophagous loops in the MAD framework \cite{alemohammad2024_mad} and Markovian generation chains \cite{geng2026_markovian}.
Subsequent work refines the conditions under which collapse occurs: \citet{bertrand2024_stability} identify convergence to a fixed point under mixed real-synthetic retraining (providing theoretical grounding for our EDD ceiling, \S\ref{sec:method:theory}), \citet{shi2025_closer_look} reframe collapse as a generalization-to-memorization transition, and \citet{dohmatob2025_strong_collapse} extend guarantees to broader model classes.
Mitigation \cite{gerstgrasser2024_accumulate,drayson2025_detection_prevents_collapse,yi2026_escaping_collapse,falahati2026_curated}, convergence analysis \cite{marchi2024_heat_death,wang2026_contamination,dohmatob2024_demystified,suresh2025_rate_collapse}, non-monotonic dynamics \cite{bakshi2026_collapse_improvement,kazdan2025_collapse_or_thrive}, and diversity decline \cite{guo2024curious,padmakumar2024diversity,sigma2026_spectral} are active areas.
\citet{schaeffer2025} argue that ``model collapse'' conflates multiple phenomena and call for operationally precise metrics; we respond by operationalizing tail-erosion predictions into a deployable ordinal classifier that reveals strategy-dependent trajectories and non-monotonic 7B behavior that the theory does not predict.
All assume depth is known a priori; we address the inverse problem of estimating depth from text alone.

\paragraph{AI Text Detection.}
The detection literature \cite{wu2025_detection_survey} spans statistical \cite{mitchell2023_detectgpt,fast_detectgpt2024,binoculars2024,diveye2026,guo2024_biscope,gehrmann2019_gltr,verma2024_ghostbuster,yang2024_dnagpt}, geometric \cite{tulchinskii2023_intrinsic_dim}, and watermarking \cite{kirchenbauer2023_watermark} methods, with known limits \cite{sadasivan2023_paraphrase,pudasaini2026_detection_fails,pu2026_generator_barrier}.
\citet{wang2023_seqxgpt} address sentence-level attribution by using log-probability features from white-box LLMs.
Shared tasks \cite{wang2024_m4_semeval,li2024_mage,bevendorff2026_pan,dugan2024_raid} benchmark detection across domains and attack vectors.
\citet{bevendorff2025_two_paradigms} distinguish attribution from verification; depth estimation introduces a third axis: recursive iteration.
All perform binary classification; our approach outputs ordinal depth labels, complementing rather than replacing detection.

\paragraph{Membership Inference and Data Provenance.}
\citet{carlini2021_extracting} demonstrate that training data can be extracted from LLMs, motivating provenance-aware pipelines.
Min-K\% Prob \cite{shi2024_minkprob} detects pretraining membership via low-probability token statistics, related to our perplexity features but limited to binary classification; Datamodels \cite{ilyas2022datamodels} trace predictions to influential training examples; cryptographically undetectable watermarks \cite{christ2024_undetectable} require generator cooperation.
TROVE \cite{zhu2025_trove} introduces fine-grained sentence-level provenance tracing with relationship classification, but targets source attribution rather than recursive depth.
Depth estimation occupies a distinct niche: ordinal, retroactive, and cooperation-free.

\paragraph{Adjacent Tasks.}
EditLens \cite{editlens2026} estimates editing extent but does not model recursive chains; \citet{uchendu2020_attribution} classify \emph{which} model generated text; \citet{mohamed2025_broken_telephone} characterize \emph{how} text degrades under iterative generation without classifying which iteration a passage comes from.
Our task performs the inverse: ordinal depth estimation from text alone.

\paragraph{Ordinal Classification.}
CORAL \cite{coral2020} enforces rank consistency via ordered binary tasks; CLOC \cite{cloc2025} extends contrastive learning with multi-margin ordinal losses; \citet{kasa2024_ordinality} benchmark ordinal techniques for NLP; \citet{janitza2016_ordinal_rf} show RF implicitly respects ordinal structure when inter-class distances are monotonic.
We adopt CORAL and CLOC as baselines (\S\ref{sec:generalization}).

\paragraph{Decoding Strategy Effects.}
Decoding strategies shape text statistics in ways that interact with depth signals \cite{holtzman2020_nucleus,finlayson2024_closing,garces_arias2025_decoding_decoded,wiher2022_decoding,basu2021_mirostat}.
Our atlas (\S\ref{sec:atlas}) shows these strategies induce qualitatively different degradation trajectories under recursive generation.

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}

The text on which large language models are trained increasingly contains their own outputs.

This model$\to$data$\to$model cycle is no longer hypothetical; it is already occurring in the wild. Yet whether the recursive generation depth of a text can be estimated from its statistical properties remains unstudied, a question that matters because first-generation synthetic text may be benign or even beneficial for training, while deeply recursive text drives the distributional collapse that degrades model quality \cite{dohmatob2024_tale_of_tails}.
We focus on the 1--1.5B parameter regime under \emph{controlled full-replacement chains}, where each generation fully replaces the prior training set, isolating the depth variable. Real-world contamination involves partial mixing at unknown proportions; full replacement provides an upper bound on depth signal strength (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).

Existing tools address adjacent but distinct problems.
Binary detectors \cite{binoculars2024,fast_detectgpt2024,diveye2026} collapse all depths $d \geq 1$ into a single category, a limitation we confirm empirically: their pairwise d1-vs-d2 AUC collapses to chance level (\S\ref{sec:gen:baselines}); watermarking \cite{kirchenbauer2023_watermark} requires proactive embedding.
The model collapse literature \cite{shumailov2024_nature,dohmatob2024_tale_of_tails} assumes depth is known a priori; \citet{drayson2025_detection_prevents_collapse} filter synthetic data via binary detection without distinguishing depths.
No existing method estimates the ordinal recursive generation depth of a text passage from its content alone (Figure~\ref{fig:problem}).

We find that recursive generation leaves quantifiable statistical fingerprints in text, and these fingerprints are \textbf{consistent in direction but scale-dependent in magnitude} across the three model families and three decoding strategies studied.
Specifically, the perplexity tail feature family (\texttt{p90\_ppl}, \texttt{p75\_ppl}, \texttt{kurtosis\_ppl}) and surprisal variance emerge as dominant depth indicators, with group-level dominance robust across all 9 model--strategy configurations and three importance measures.
Our contribution centers on task formalization and systematic empirical characterization; the convergence of four classifiers within 0.8\,pp (\S\ref{sec:gen:baselines}) confirms that signal resides in feature design, not classifier architecture.

To characterize how recursive generation reshapes these features, we construct the \emph{Depth Degradation Atlas}: a $3 \times 3$ grid of model families $\times$ decoding strategies spanning 4 depths (180K cell-instances).

\begin{abstract}
As language models increasingly train on web text containing their own outputs, a recursive model$\to$data$\to$model loop arises, yet no method estimates how many such iterations a text has undergone.
We formalize \emph{recursive generation depth estimation} as ordinal classification and construct a benchmark of 180K cell-instances (140K unique passages) spanning three model families, three decoding strategies, and four depths under controlled full-replacement chains at the 1--1.5B parameter scale.
A lightweight pipeline (19 statistical features classified by Random Forest) achieves d1--d3 balanced accuracy of 59--82\% across nine model--strategy cells, with $\mathrm{EDD}_{0.70} = 3$ in 8/9 cells.
Three findings emerge: (1)~depth signal concentrates in perplexity distribution tails, corroborated by classifier convergence and independent cross-perplexity features; (2)~decoding strategy affects cross-condition transfer more than model architecture, suggesting structurally distinct degradation trajectories; (3)~signal attenuates with scale (14B cross-reference accuracy ${\sim}44$\%, $\mathrm{EDD}_{0.70}{=}2$ for nucleus and temperature, 0 for top-$k$), with reference-model choice accounting for ${\sim}7$\,pp of the apparent degradation.
Our depth estimation claims hold most strongly within-strategy or when the decoding configuration is known; a two-stage routing pipeline recovers $+$11.5\,pp under cross-strategy transfer.
Perturbation-based and membership-inference baselines lack ordinal depth resolution, confirming that depth estimation requires distributional statistics beyond binary detection scores.
\end{abstract}

\section*{Limitations}
\label{sec:limitations}

\paragraph{Full-replacement vs.\ accumulation.}
The primary benchmark uses full-replacement chains; real-world contamination involves accumulation at unknown mixing ratios \cite{gerstgrasser2024_accumulate}.
Accumulation experiments (Appendix~\ref{app:accumulation_auc}) show accuracy attenuation that increases with higher synthetic mixing ratios, and do not test cross-strategy accumulation; extension to larger models and higher mixing ratios remains future work.

\paragraph{Scale, generalization, and reference model.}
Depth signal attenuates at larger scales (\S\ref{sec:gen:crossscale}), with reference-model mismatch contributing to the observed degradation.
Cross-strategy transfer can invert adjacent-depth predictions when the classifier's training strategy differs from the test data, requiring strategy-aware deployment.
The pipeline requires a fixed reference model; cross-architecture references degrade accuracy (Appendix~\ref{app:ref_ablation}).
BOS-seeded generation differs from prompted generation by 13.8\,pp (Appendix~\ref{app:prompted_gen}), so measured depth signals may partly reflect unconditional generation artifacts.
Additional caveats (single LoRA seed, web-crawl false positive rates, passage length sensitivity) are detailed in the Appendix.

\section*{Ethics Statement}

This work uses publicly available pretrained language models (Pythia-1.4B, OLMo-1B, GPT-2~XL) and Wikipedia text as seed data.
No human subjects were involved, no private or sensitive data were collected, and no new models were released.
Our method is intended to support data provenance and training-data auditing; we acknowledge that depth estimation tools could in principle be misused to circumvent content moderation, though such risks are shared with all detection-oriented research.
Code and data will be released upon acceptance.
AI assistants were used in an auxiliary role for coding support and language polishing.
All scientific decisions, experimental design, analysis, and core writing were conducted by the authors.
